title: Λέων ⟨ἐρασθεὶς⟩ καὶ γεωργός
titleEn: The Lion in Love and the Farmer
part: The Lion in Love and the Farmer (Chambry 198 · Perry 140)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 198 (= Perry 140). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Λέων ἐρασθεὶς γεωργοῦ θυγατρός, ταύτην ἐμνηστεύσατο.
sentences.tr: Leōn erastheis geōrgou thygatros, tautēn emnēsteusato.
sentences.l: A lion, having fallen in love with a farmer's daughter, sought her hand.
sentences.n: ἐράω takes the genitive of the person loved, and its aorist ἐρασθείς is passive in form but active in sense — love is something one undergoes. μνηστεύομαι in the middle is the suitor's own word: to court a woman for himself. Chambry's ⟨ἐρασθείς⟩ in the title is his supplement, distinguishing this fable from the Lion who was shut in.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ μὴ ἐκδοῦναι θηρίῳ τὴν θυγατέρα ὑπομένων, μηδὲ ἀρνήσασθαι διὰ φόβον δυνάμενος τοιοῦτόν τι ἐπενόησεν.
sentences.tr: Ho de mē ekdounai thēriōi tēn thygatera hypomenōn, mēde arnēsasthai dia phobon dynamenos toiouton ti epenoēsen.
sentences.l: And he, not bringing himself to give his daughter to a wild beast, nor being able to refuse for fear, devised something of this sort.
sentences.n: ἐκδίδωμι is the technical verb for a father's giving a daughter in marriage — handing her out of his house into another's. ὑπομένω with the infinitive is 'to endure to do', to bring oneself to it. The two participles set the trap the plot must escape: he cannot consent and he cannot refuse.

sentences.t: Ἐπειδὴ συνεχῶς αὐτῷ ὁ λέων ἐπέκειτο, ἔλεγεν ὡς νυμφίον μὲν αὐτὸν ἄξιον τῆς θυγατρὸς δοκιμάζει· μὴ ἄλλως δὲ αὐτῷ δύνασθαι ἐκδοῦναι, ἐὰν μὴ τούς τε ὀδόντας ἐξέλῃ καὶ τοὺς ὄνυχας ἐκτέμῃ· τούτους γὰρ δεδοικέναι τὴν κόρην.
sentences.tr: Epeidē synechōs autōi ho leōn epekeito, elegen hōs nymphion men auton axion tēs thygatros dokimazei· mē allōs de autōi dynasthai ekdounai, ean mē tous te odontas exelēi kai tous onychas ektemēi· toutous gar dedoikenai tēn korēn.
sentences.l: Since the lion kept pressing him without let-up, he said that he judged him a bridegroom worthy of his daughter, but that he could not give her to him otherwise, unless he should take out his teeth and cut away his claws; for the girl feared these.
sentences.i: As the lion kept pressing him without let-up, he said he found him a bridegroom worthy of his daughter, but that he could not hand her over unless he had his teeth drawn and his claws cut away — those, he said, were what the girl was afraid of.
sentences.n: ἐπίκειμαι with the dative is to lie heavy upon a man, to keep at him. The reported speech begins with ὡς and an indicative (δοκιμάζει), then slips into accusative-and-infinitive (δύνασθαι, δεδοικέναι) — a shift this Greek makes freely, and the reader simply keeps hearing 'he said that…' over the whole run. δεδοικέναι is a perfect with present force: to have taken fright and so to be afraid.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ ῥᾳδίως διὰ τὸν ἔρωτα ἑκάτερα ὑπομείναντος, ὁ γεωργὸς καταφρονήσας αὐτοῦ, ὡς παρεγένετο πρὸς αὐτόν, ῥοπάλοις αὐτὸν παίων ἐξήλασεν.
sentences.tr: Tou de rhāidiōs dia ton erōta hekatera hypomeinantos, ho geōrgos kataphronēsas autou, hōs paregeneto pros auton, rhopalois auton paiōn exēlasen.
sentences.l: And he having readily submitted to both, for love's sake, the farmer, now despising him, when he came to him, beating him with clubs drove him out.
sentences.i: He submitted to both readily enough, for love; and the farmer, holding him now in contempt, beat him with clubs when he came, and drove him off.
sentences.n: Another genitive absolute, and the hinge of the fable: everything before it the lion still has, everything after it he does not. ἑκάτερα, neuter plural, is 'each of the two things' — teeth and claws counted separately, as the farmer had asked. καταφρονέω takes the genitive of the person looked down on.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι οἱ ῥᾳδίως τοῖς πέλας πιστεύοντες, ὅταν τῶν ἰδίων πλεονεκτημάτων ἑαυτοὺς ἀπογυμνώσωσιν, εὐάλωτοι τούτοις γίνονται οἷς πρότερον φοβεροὶ καθεστήκεσαν.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti hoi rhāidiōs tois pelas pisteuontes, hotan tōn idiōn pleonektēmatōn heautous apogymnōsōsin, eualōtoi toutois ginontai hois proteron phoberoi kathestēkesan.
sentences.l: The story shows that those who readily trust their neighbours, whenever they strip themselves bare of their own advantages, become easy prey to those to whom they had before stood formidable.
sentences.i: The story shows that those who trust their neighbours too readily, once they have stripped themselves of the advantages that were their own, become easy prey to the very people who had feared them before.
sentences.n: οἱ πέλας, 'those nearby', is the ordinary Greek for one's neighbours. ἀπογυμνόω takes the genitive of what one is stripped of, the case of separation. πλεονέκτημα is the advantage a man holds over others — for a lion, the teeth and claws. καθεστήκεσαν is a pluperfect of καθίστημι used of a standing condition: they had stood as objects of fear.
